title: The order extractor that warns you when it breaks
pitch: Takes the order emails that come in every day and turns them into clean records (company, references, quantities, delivery date, urgency) ready to load into your system without typing anything. And it brings its own quality control: eight real emails with the correct answer written by hand, which run in half a minute and tell you whether the system still works or something changed under the hood.
outcome: A folder that runs on your computer with two commands. One turns an email into validated JSON; the other gives you a score out of 8, the detail of which field failed on which case, and a report with date, version, model, and cost. You can show both prompt versions, each one's score, and explain why the second one wins. That's what separates "I know how to use ChatGPT" from "I built this and I know the day it stops working."
requires: Python 3.10 or higher. Check by typing python3 --version in the terminal (on Windows, py --version). If you don't have it, or have an older one, it's a free download from python.org.

An account at platform.claude.com with balance. There's no free plan: the minimum top-up is $5, about €4.60. The entire project, including all tests and comparisons, spends less than 10 cents of that.
A text editor for code. VS Code is free and more than enough. Word doesn't work: it inserts invisible formatting that breaks files.
Knowing how to open your system's terminal and move between folders with cd. Nothing else. No need to have ever programmed before.

structure.what: The libraries the project needs, with their version, so someone else can set it up identically on their computer.
Your API key, and nothing else. Never shared, never pushed anywhere, and never appears written in any other file.
The exact shape the record has to have: what fields, what type each one is, and what values are allowed. The project's contract.
Every version of the job, with the active one marked at the top. An old version never gets deleted.
The program that does the work: calls the model, validates the answer, and retries once explaining the exact error.
The eight test emails with the correct record written by hand. The memory of what the system has to know how to do.
Runs the cases, gives a score, says which field failed on which case, and exits with an error if the score drops below the threshold.
Generated by the tester on its own: version, model, score, cost, and failures from the latest batch. Used to compare against the next one.

steps.title: Set up the folder, the environment, and the key
steps.why: Before writing a line of logic, two things need to be settled for good: where the project lives and where the key lives. The key never gets written inside the code, because code gets shared and pushed places; it goes in a separate file that never leaves your computer. Five minutes now saves you a burned key later. About money: the Anthropic API has no free plan, the minimum top-up is $5 (about €4.60), and this entire project, tests included, doesn't reach 10 cents. Before anything else, go into the console's limits section and set yourself a $5 monthly cap: no surprises that way.
steps.code:
# 1. The project folder. Everything will live inside here.
mkdir extractor-emails
cd extractor-emails

# 2. The virtual environment: a box of libraries just for this project.
#    A library is code other people already wrote that you reuse.
#    Without the box, all your projects' libraries mix and one day something breaks.
python3 -m venv .venv        # macOS and Linux
# py -m venv .venv           # Windows: delete the # and use this one

# 3. Activate the box. Again, only the line for your system:
source .venv/bin/activate    # macOS and Linux
# .venv\Scripts\activate     # Windows (PowerShell)

# From here on, plain "python" works on both systems: inside the activated
# environment it points to the box's own copy. You'll notice because (.venv)
# shows up before the cursor.

# 4. The four libraries we need.
#    anthropic: talk to the model. pydantic: check the shape of the result.
#    python-dotenv: read the key without writing it. PyYAML: read .yaml files.
pip install "anthropic>=0.40" "pydantic>=2.7" "python-dotenv>=1.0" "PyYAML>=6.0"

# 5. Write down what you installed, so you can set it up the same elsewhere.
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# 6. The API key. An API is the door your program talks to the model through;
#    the key is your key to that door, and whoever has it spends your money.
#    Get it at platform.claude.com, under API Keys.
#    Replace sk-ant-PASTE-YOUR-KEY-HERE with yours and run this line:
echo "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-PASTE-YOUR-KEY-HERE" > .env

# 7. So the key never ends up pushed to the internet:
echo ".env" > .gitignore
echo ".venv/" >> .gitignore

# 8. Check everything is in place.
python -c "import anthropic, pydantic, yaml, dotenv; print('Everything installed')"
steps.expected: The last line prints "Everything installed". If you list the folder (ls -a on macOS and Linux, dir on Windows) you see .env, .gitignore, requirements.txt, and the .venv folder.
steps.trouble: If you get "python3 is not recognized", on Windows the command is py: use py -m venv .venv. If that's not recognized either, Python isn't installed or you didn't check "Add python.exe to PATH" during install; reinstall from python.org and check it this time. SERIOUS WARNING: if you ever push .env to GitHub, the key stays burned even if you delete the file afterward, because the history keeps it. The only fix is to revoke it in the console and get a new one. There's no undo.

steps.title: Write the exact shape of the result, before the prompt
steps.why: The beginner's mistake is writing the prompt first and seeing what comes out. It's done backwards: first you decide what fields your system needs and what values each one accepts, then you write the job to get those. A schema is that list of fields with their types; validating is checking the answer against it before using it. This file is the contract, and notice it never calls the model: you can run it a thousand times without spending a cent.
steps.code:
"""The exact shape the record returned by the model has to have.

This is a SCHEMA: the list of fields, what type each one is, and what values
are allowed. If the model's answer doesn't fit, the program stops RIGHT HERE,
with a message saying which field is wrong. Without this, corrupt data enters
your system silently and you discover it three weeks later.

It's written before the prompt. The schema is the contract; the prompt is
just the way to get the model to meet it.
"""

import re

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
from typing import Literal

# YYYY-MM-DD and nothing else. 04/05/2026 doesn't work: it's ambiguous in half the world.
FECHA_ISO = re.compile(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$")


class Linea(BaseModel):
    """A product ordered: the reference and how many units."""

    referencia: str
    cantidad: int = Field(ge=1)  # ge=1 means "one or more". Ordering 0 doesn't exist.


class Pedido(BaseModel):
    """The full record extracted from an email."""

    # extra="forbid": if the model makes up a field we didn't ask for,
    # that's also a failure. An extra field today is a field someone uses
    # tomorrow without knowing it isn't guaranteed.
    model_config = {"extra": "forbid"}

    empresa: str
    contacto_email: str
    # Literal = only these four words. Not "urgent", not "inquiry".
    tipo: Literal["pedido", "presupuesto", "incidencia", "otro"]
    lineas: list[Linea]
    # None is Python for "not stated". It isn't the same as "" or 0.
    fecha_entrega: str | None = None
    urgente: bool
    importe_total_eur: float | None = None

    @field_validator("contacto_email")
    @classmethod
    def parece_un_email(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if "@" not in v or "." not in v.split("@")[-1]:
            raise ValueError(f"'{v}' doesn't look like an email")
        return v

    @field_validator("fecha_entrega")
    @classmethod
    def fecha_en_formato_iso(cls, v: str | None) -> str | None:
        if v is not None and not FECHA_ISO.match(v):
            raise ValueError(f"'{v}' isn't in YYYY-MM-DD format")
        return v


# Quick test without spending a cent: this calls no model at all.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    bueno = Pedido(
        empresa="Talleres Ruiz",
        contacto_email="marta@talleresruiz.es",
        tipo="pedido",
        lineas=[{"referencia": "FR-220", "cantidad": 40}],
        fecha_entrega="2026-05-05",
        urgente=False,
        importe_total_eur=None,
    )
    print("Valid record:", bueno.model_dump())

    try:
        Pedido(
            empresa="Talleres Ruiz",
            contacto_email="marta-at-talleresruiz",
            tipo="consulta",
            lineas=[],
            fecha_entrega="05/05/2026",
            urgente=False,
        )
    except Exception as e:
        print("\nAnd here's how it fails when something doesn't fit:")
        print(e)
steps.expected: First it prints a valid record, then below three named errors: the email without an @, the "consulta" type that's not among the four allowed, and the date written as 05/05/2026. That's exactly what you want to see: it fails fast and says why.
steps.trouble: "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named pydantic" means the virtual environment isn't active; you'll notice because the terminal doesn't start with (.venv). Reactivate it with the line from step 1. If the error is a syntax error on the line str | None, you have Python 3.9 or older and need 3.10 or higher.

steps.title: The prompt outside the code, and in two versions
steps.why: A prompt hidden inside the program is a prompt nobody can compare. Pulling it into a separate file gets you three things: changing it without touching the code, having several versions alive at once, and being able to say "v2 gets 8 of 8 and v1 gets 5". These two versions aren't for show. v1 is what anyone would write on day one. v2 is the same task with what actually moves the needle: a closed field list, an explicit order not to invent, today's date to resolve "within two weeks", and a worked example.
steps.code:
# Every version of the job lives here, in a YAML file.
# YAML is a text format for storing configuration: it reads almost like a
# shopping list, and what matters is the two-space indentation.
#
# Project rule: a version that has already run is NEVER deleted or edited.
# The next one gets added below it and the "active" line changes. That way,
# the day something gets worse, you can go back and know exactly what changed.

activa: v2

versiones:

  v1:
    fecha: "2026-03-02"
    nota: "First attempt, written the way you'd ask a coworker."
    system: |
      You extract data from business emails and return JSON.
    usuario: |
      Extract this email's data and return it as JSON.

      EMAIL:
      {email}

  v2:
    fecha: "2026-03-09"
    nota: >
      Adds the closed field list, the order not to invent, today's date to
      resolve "within two weeks", and a worked example.
      Fixes emails with multiple references and amounts with a comma.
    system: |
      You are a clerk who unpacks customer emails into a record.

      You ALWAYS return a single valid JSON object and nothing else: no
      greeting, no explanation, no ```json around it.

      If a fact doesn't appear in the email, you put null. You don't infer
      it from context, you don't estimate it, you don't fill it with a
      reasonable value. A null is correct information; a made-up fact is a
      wrongly issued invoice.
    usuario: |
      Unpack this email into the record.

      FIELDS (exactly these seven, not one more, not one less):
      - empresa: text. The name of the company writing, not the person's name.
      - contacto_email: text. The email address of whoever signed the email.
      - tipo: one of these four exact words: "pedido", "presupuesto",
        "incidencia", "otro".
      - lineas: list of objects with "referencia" (text) and "cantidad" (integer,
        minimum 1). Empty list [] if the email doesn't ask for any product.
      - fecha_entrega: text "YYYY-MM-DD", or null if the email doesn't say when.
        Today is {hoy}: use it to resolve "within two weeks" or "on the 24th".
      - urgente: true or false. true ONLY if the email says so in words
        ("urgent", "asap", "right away", "we're at a standstill"). A near date
        alone is not urgency.
      - importe_total_eur: number, or null. Only if the email gives a total
        figure in euros. In Spanish the decimal uses a comma: 2.480,50 is 2480.50.

      WORKED EXAMPLE
      Email: "Hi, this is Marta from Talleres Ruiz (marta@talleresruiz.es).
      I need 40 FR-220 filters and 12 CB-8 belts by May 5th. Thanks."
      Answer: {"empresa": "Talleres Ruiz", "contacto_email": "marta@talleresruiz.es", "tipo": "pedido", "lineas": [{"referencia": "FR-220", "cantidad": 40}, {"referencia": "CB-8", "cantidad": 12}], "fecha_entrega": "2026-05-05", "urgente": false, "importe_total_eur": null}

      EMAIL TO PROCESS:
      {email}
steps.expected:
Still nothing to run, it's a text file. To check it's written correctly, this command has to print ['v1', 'v2']:
python -c "import yaml;print(list(yaml.safe_load(open('prompts.yaml',encoding='utf-8'))['versiones']))"
steps.trouble: The mistake 90% of the time is indentation. In YAML, spaces rule and tabs don't work. If your editor inserts a tab when you press Tab, you'll see an error like "found character that cannot start any token". In VS Code, bottom right it says "Tab Size": click there and choose "Indent Using Spaces".

steps.title: The extractor: call, validate, and retry exactly once
steps.why: This is where it all comes together. The interesting part isn't the call to the model, which is six lines: it's what happens when the answer comes back wrong. This program doesn't repeat the same question (repeating it gives the same bad answer), it shows the model its own answer and the validator's exact error. One retry, not ten: if it still can't fix it with the error in front of it, the problem is the prompt, not luck. And it always returns the same shape (ok, datos, error, version, tokens, and cost) so whoever uses it never has to guess.
steps.code:
"""Turns an email into a validated JSON record.

The path, top to bottom:
  1. Loads the active prompt version from prompts.yaml.
  2. Sends it to the model along with the email.
  3. Trims the JSON out of the answer and runs it through the schema.
  4. If something doesn't fit, retries ONCE telling the model what was wrong.
     Blindly repeating the same question gives the same bad answer.
  5. Always returns the same thing: a dict with ok, datos, error, tokens,
     and coste. Never raises an exception over a bad model answer.

Usage:
    python extractor.py                 # with the example email below
    python extractor.py my_email.txt    # with your own email
"""

import json
import os
import sys
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import anthropic
import yaml
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from pydantic import ValidationError

from esquema import Pedido

load_dotenv()  # reads the .env file and puts the key into the environment

CARPETA = Path(__file__).parent
MODELO = "claude-haiku-4-5"

# Price per million tokens, in dollars. A token is a chunk of a word:
# about 750 words per 1,000 tokens. These numbers CHANGE: that's why
# they're here at the top with the date, not scattered through the code.
# Noted on 2026-03-09.
PRECIO_ENTRADA_USD = 0.80
PRECIO_SALIDA_USD = 4.00
USD_A_EUR = 0.92

EMAIL_DEMO = """From: nuria.blanco@hostelsur.es
Subject: Restock

Good morning:
I'm Nuria Blanco, from Hostelería del Sur. We need 120 units of reference
VS-450 and 30 of VS-900. It's urgent: our walk-in fridge has broken down
and we're at a standstill. We need it within two weeks at the latest.
Thanks.
"""

_cliente = None


def cliente():
    """Creates the client once and reuses it across every call."""
    global _cliente
    if _cliente is None:
        clave = os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
        if not clave:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Can't find ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Check the .env file exists "
                "and that you're running the program from the "
                "extractor-emails folder."
            )
        _cliente = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=clave)
    return _cliente


def coste_eur(entrada, salida):
    """What an extraction cost, in euros."""
    usd = (entrada * PRECIO_ENTRADA_USD + salida * PRECIO_SALIDA_USD) / 1_000_000
    return round(usd * USD_A_EUR, 6)


def cargar_prompt(version=None):
    """Returns (name, system text, user message template)."""
    datos = yaml.safe_load((CARPETA / "prompts.yaml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    nombre = version or datos["activa"]
    if nombre not in datos["versiones"]:
        disponibles = ", ".join(datos["versiones"])
        raise RuntimeError(f"Version '{nombre}' doesn't exist. Available: {disponibles}")
    v = datos["versiones"][nombre]
    return nombre, v["system"], v["usuario"]


def solo_json(texto):
    """Keeps just the JSON object even if it arrives wrapped in text or ```."""
    t = texto.strip()
    if t.startswith("```"):
        t = t.split("```")[1]
        if t.startswith("json"):
            t = t[4:]
    ini, fin = t.find("{"), t.rfind("}")
    if ini == -1 or fin == -1:
        raise ValueError("The answer contains no JSON object")
    return t[ini:fin + 1]


def extraer(email, version=None, hoy=None):
    """Email in, validated record out. Never crashes."""
    nombre, system, plantilla = cargar_prompt(version)
    hoy = hoy or date.today().isoformat()

    # We fill the prompt's placeholders with .replace and not .format:
    # the prompt has braces inside it (the JSON example) and .format would break them.
    usuario = plantilla.replace("{hoy}", hoy).replace("{email}", email)

    mensajes = [{"role": "user", "content": usuario}]
    entrada = salida = 0
    ultimo_error = ""

    for intento in (1, 2):
        r = cliente().messages.create(
            model=MODELO,
            max_tokens=1000,
            temperature=0,  # 0 = always picks the most likely option: same email,
                            # same record. For automated processes, always 0.
            system=system,
            messages=mensajes,
        )
        texto = r.content[0].text
        entrada += r.usage.input_tokens
        salida += r.usage.output_tokens

        try:
            ficha = Pedido.model_validate(json.loads(solo_json(texto)))
            return {
                "ok": True,
                "datos": ficha.model_dump(),
                "error": None,
                "version": nombre,
                "intentos": intento,
                "tokens": {"entrada": entrada, "salida": salida},
                "coste_eur": coste_eur(entrada, salida),
            }
        except (ValueError, ValidationError) as e:
            ultimo_error = str(e)
            if intento == 2:
                break
            # Second attempt: we show it its own answer and the exact error.
            mensajes = mensajes + [
                {"role": "assistant", "content": texto},
                {
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": (
                        "That JSON isn't valid. The validator says:\n"
                        f"{ultimo_error}\n"
                        "Return ONLY the corrected JSON object, nothing else."
                    ),
                },
            ]

    return {
        "ok": False,
        "datos": None,
        "error": ultimo_error,
        "version": nombre,
        "intentos": 2,
        "tokens": {"entrada": entrada, "salida": salida},
        "coste_eur": coste_eur(entrada, salida),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        texto_email = Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    else:
        texto_email = EMAIL_DEMO
    print(json.dumps(extraer(texto_email), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))
steps.expected: You don't run it yet, that's the next step. For now it's enough that the file gets saved and the editor doesn't mark anything in red.

steps.title: The first real extraction
steps.why: An email goes in, a record comes out. When you see it, look at the end of the response, not the data: it tells you which prompt version was used, how many attempts it took, and what it cost. Watching the cost from the very first call is what separates someone who knows what they'll be billed from someone who finds out at the end of the month.
steps.code:

python esquema.py

# And now the first real call to the model with the example email.
# This call costs about 0.001 EUR. Yes, a thousandth of a euro.
python extractor.py

# With your own email: save it as my_email.txt inside the folder

# and pass it as an argument:

steps.expected: A JSON with "ok": true and Hostelería del Sur's record: its two references (VS-450 with 120 units and VS-900 with 30), "urgente": true because the email says "we're at a standstill", a delivery date two weeks ahead of today, "version": "v2", "intentos": 1, and a cost around 0.001 EUR.
steps.trouble: "authentication_error" means the key isn't coming through or is invalid: check .env has no quotes or spaces around the value and that you pasted the whole key. On Windows, if printing accents gives "UnicodeEncodeError", type set PYTHONUTF8=1 in that same terminal first.

steps.title: The eight cases, with the answer written by hand
steps.why: This is the best-spent hour in the whole project, and the one almost nobody does. Without cases, "the prompt is good" is an opinion; with cases, it's 7 of 8. What matters is that you write the correct answer yourself: ask the model for it and you're not checking anything, you're asking whether it likes itself. And half of them are deliberate traps, because an easy case only confirms what you already knew: a date that isn't there and shouldn't be invented, urgency that isn't urgency, an amount with the Spanish decimal comma, and a complaint email where no product is requested.
steps.code:
# The eight test cases.
#
# Each one has three things: the email exactly as it would arrive, the date
# it's assumed to have been received on (so "within two weeks" always means
# the same thing), and the correct record WRITTEN BY YOU BY HAND.
#
# That last part isn't a detail: if the model writes the correct answer for
# you, you're not checking anything, you're asking whether it likes itself.
#
# Four of the eight are deliberate traps: dates that aren't there, urgency
# that isn't urgency, an amount with a Spanish comma, and an email with no
# products. An easy case confirms what you already knew; a trap teaches you something.

steps.title: The tester that warns you when something breaks
steps.why: The file that turns this into a professional piece of work. It runs the eight cases, compares field by field, tells you what failed and where, saves a report with date, version, model, score, and cost, and exits with an error if it drops below the threshold. That final error is what later lets you hook it up to an automatic alert. Notice the only two concessions it makes when comparing: the company name allows an extra "S.L.", and the order of the lines doesn't matter. Both are written with their reason right next to them. Everything else is compared as-is, no slack: the moment you start forgiving things, the tests stop being useful.
steps.code:
"""Runs the eight cases against one prompt version and gives a score.

This is what turns the project into something professional. It's useful for
two things you can't do by eye:

  1. Knowing whether a prompt change makes things better or worse, BEFORE
     using it with real customers. "It feels better" is a feeling; 7 of 8
     is a fact.
  2. Finding out the provider changed the model from a red test on a Tuesday
     morning, not from a customer's phone call.

Usage:
    python probar.py        # the version marked active in prompts.yaml
    python probar.py v1     # a specific version, to compare
"""

import json
import sys
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

from extractor import MODELO, extraer

CARPETA = Path(__file__).parent
INFORME = CARPETA / "ultimo_informe.json"

# Below this score, the prompt doesn't leave your computer.
# 0.85 over 8 cases means: at most one failure.
UMBRAL = 0.85


def igual(campo, esperado, obtenido):
    """Compares a field. Two concessions, and only two, each with its reason."""
    if campo == "empresa":
        # "Talleres Ruiz" and "Talleres Ruiz S.L." are the same company.
        a, b = str(esperado).lower(), str(obtenido).lower()
        return a in b or b in a
    if campo == "lineas":
        # The order it lists products in doesn't matter.
        def clave(linea):
            return (linea["referencia"].upper(), linea["cantidad"])

        return sorted(map(clave, esperado)) == sorted(map(clave, obtenido))
    # Everything else is compared as-is. No slack.
    return esperado == obtenido


def main():
    version = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None
    casos = yaml.safe_load((CARPETA / "casos.yaml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    # We read the previous report BEFORE overwriting it, so we can compare.
    anterior = None
    if INFORME.exists():
        anterior = json.loads(INFORME.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    aciertos = 0
    coste = 0.0
    fallos = []
    nombre_version = version or "?"

    for caso in casos:
        r = extraer(caso["email"], version=version, hoy=caso["hoy"])
        coste += r["coste_eur"]
        nombre_version = r["version"]

        if not r["ok"]:
            print(f"  FAIL   {caso['id']}  -> did not return valid JSON")
            print(f"         {r['error'][:160]}")
            fallos.append({
                "caso": caso["id"],
                "motivo": "invalid json",
                "detalle": r["error"][:400],
            })
            continue

        malos = [
            c for c in caso["esperado"]
            if not igual(c, caso["esperado"][c], r["datos"][c])
        ]

        if malos:
            print(f"  FAIL   {caso['id']}")
            for c in malos:
                print(f"         {c}: expected {caso['esperado'][c]!r}, "
                      f"got {r['datos'][c]!r}")
            fallos.append({
                "caso": caso["id"],
                "motivo": "different fields",
                "campos": {
                    c: {"esperaba": caso["esperado"][c], "obtuvo": r["datos"][c]}
                    for c in malos
                },
            })
        else:
            aciertos += 1
            print(f"  OK     {caso['id']}  (attempts: {r['intentos']})")

    total = len(casos)
    tasa = aciertos / total

    print()
    print(f"Version {nombre_version} with {MODELO}: {aciertos}/{total} "
          f"({tasa:.0%})")
    print(f"Cost of this batch: {coste:.4f} EUR")

    if anterior:
        print(f"Previous batch: version {anterior['version']}, "
              f"{anterior['aciertos']}/{anterior['total']}")
        if tasa < anterior["tasa"]:
            print("WARNING: you've gotten WORSE compared to the previous batch.")
            print("         Check above which cases fell before you publish anything.")

    # Note: this overwrites the previous report. If you want to keep history,
    # rename the file before running the batch again.
    INFORME.write_text(
        json.dumps({
            "fecha": datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
            "version": nombre_version,
            "modelo": MODELO,
            "aciertos": aciertos,
            "total": total,
            "tasa": tasa,
            "coste_eur": round(coste, 6),
            "fallos": fallos,
        }, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    print(f"Report saved to {INFORME.name}")

    if tasa < UMBRAL:
        print(f"\nBELOW THE THRESHOLD ({UMBRAL:.0%}). This does not get published.")
        sys.exit(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.expected: Run python probar.py. You'll see eight lines of OK or FAIL, the final score (with v2 you should get 7 or 8 of 8), the batch's cost around 0.01 EUR, and a new file called ultimo_informe.json.
steps.trouble: If a case always fails on the same field, don't touch the tester. Either the model is genuinely getting it wrong and the prompt needs improving, or the answer you wrote by hand was wrong. Both are findings. What's not okay is loosening the comparison so it turns green. Also watch out: every run overwrites ultimo_informe.json, so if you want to keep the history, rename it before running again.

steps.title: Compare v1 against v2 and decide with a number
steps.why: This is where you see what all the above was for. The same batch of eight cases against both versions, one after the other, and two numbers on the table. It's the difference between saying "I think the new prompt is better" and saying "v1 fails the date cases and the one with the comma-decimal amount; v2 passes them". With the second sentence you can defend your work in front of a client.
steps.code:
# The same batch of eight cases, against both prompt versions.
# Each batch is 8 calls to the model: less than a cent.

python probar.py v1
python probar.py v2

# If you want the detail of the last batch, which field failed on which case:
python -c "import json;print(json.dumps(json.load(open('ultimo_informe.json',encoding='utf-8'))['fallos'],ensure_ascii=False,indent=2))"

# And this is the part that matters: the version that wins goes into the
# "activa" line of prompts.yaml. Open it, check it says the one you decided
# on, and don't delete the one that lost. An old prompt is the only proof of what changed.
steps.expected: v1 fails several cases, almost always the relative-date one, the two-reference email, and the comma-decimal amount one. v2 passes them. The exact numbers bounce a bit between runs and that's fine: what matters is the gap between the two and being able to point to which cases it's in.
steps.trouble: If v1 gets the same score as v2, your cases are too easy. Add two harder ones: an email with three references mixed into a paragraph, and another where the date is written as "toward the end of the month". Tests that can't tell a bad prompt from a good one aren't measuring anything.

steps.title: Break it on purpose to see the alarm go off
steps.why: One thing's missing, and it's what separates real tests from decoration: checking they turn red when they should. We add a third version, deliberately vague, the kind someone in a hurry would write, and run it through the same eight cases. What you see on screen is exactly what you'll see the day the provider updates the model and your prompt stops working the same way. Finding out this way, on a Tuesday morning, with the detail of which field changed, is the whole value of this project.
steps.code:
# Paste this block AT THE END of prompts.yaml, keeping the two-space
  # indentation at the start of each line (it goes inside "versiones", same
  # as v1 and v2). Don't touch the "activa" line: it stays v2.
  #
  # This is a deliberately bad prompt. It's for checking something almost
  # nobody checks: that your safety net REALLY turns red when something's
  # wrong. Tests that always pass aren't tests, they're decoration.

  v3_broken:
    fecha: "2026-03-10"
    nota: "Vague on purpose. Just to see the tester go red. Do not use."
    system: |
      You extract data from emails and return JSON.
    usuario: |
      Pull out the important data from this email:

      {email}
steps.expected: With the block pasted at the end of prompts.yaml, run python probar.py v3_broken. It comes back with a much worse score (normally 2 or 3 of 8), prints the specific fields that fail, warns you it got worse than the previous batch, and finishes with "BELOW THE THRESHOLD". The active line stays v2, so your extractor was never affected.
steps.trouble: If v3_broken scores well, it's not that the vague prompt works: it's that your cases aren't demanding enough. This usually happens when every email is written equally clearly. Grab two real emails from your inbox, with their messiness and typos, and add them. When you're done you can delete the v3_broken block or leave it there: since it's not the active one, it doesn't bother anyone.

checks: python extractor.py returns a JSON with "ok": true without you having to touch anything, and if you search for your key inside the .py and .yaml files, it doesn't appear in any of them.
python probar.py v1 and python probar.py v2 give different scores, and you can say out loud which specific cases separate one version from the other.
At least two of the eight cases check that the model does NOT invent: a field that must come out null because the email doesn't say it, and a near date that doesn't mean urgency.
If you change the schema to require a field the prompt doesn't ask for, the tester turns red. If it doesn't turn red, your tests aren't checking what you think they're checking.
ultimo_informe.json exists and says which version, which model, which score, and what it cost, with date and time. It's what you show when someone asks whether this really works.
The .env is inside .gitignore, and v1 is still in prompts.yaml: you didn't delete it while writing v2.
extend: Feed the collection with real failures, not imagined ones. Every time an email from your inbox gives an odd result, turn it into a new case with the correct record written by hand. In six months you'll have forty cases, and they'll be exactly the forty that matter.

Hook it up to the inbox: read the emails under a specific Gmail label, extract the record, and dump it into a spreadsheet. Start read-only, with no marking, deleting, or replying to anything. A program with permission to delete emails is a program that eventually deletes one it shouldn't have, and that doesn't undo.

Route by cost: run everything through claude-haiku-4-5 and send to claude-sonnet-4-5 only the emails whose answer doesn't pass the schema. The tester tells you whether it's really worth it on your data. Typically nine out of ten get resolved by the cheap one, which costs almost four times less per input token.
defend: "You already ask the model for JSON in the prompt, why validate it afterward?" — Because asking isn't guaranteeing. With temperature 0 and a tight prompt it gets the format right almost every time, and that "almost" is the Friday failure nobody can reproduce. The schema turns corrupt data entering the database into an immediate error that says which field and why. I also wrote it before the prompt: the schema is the contract, and the prompt is just the way to get it met.

"How do you know your prompt hasn't gotten worse?" — Eight cases with hand-written answers, one batch before and one after every change, and a saved report with version, model, score, cost, and date. Without that, "it's better" is an opinion. And that same tester is the alarm for the day the provider quietly updates the model: I find out from a red test, not from a customer's phone call.

"The system gets 92% right and the client wants 100%." — 100% doesn't exist in automated extraction, and that's not the goal: the goal is that the 8% detects itself. Whatever doesn't pass the schema gets flagged and goes to a human review queue. What I'm selling is "out of 300 emails a day, 275 go through on their own and 25 show up in a list to review in ten minutes", not "always correct". And with the test cases I can show exactly what kind of email is the one that fails.
